'''''Philadelphus lewisii''','' the '''Lewis' mock-orange''', '''mock-orange''', '''Gordon's mockorange''', '''wild mockorange,'''<ref name="USDA_2003_mockorange" /> '''Indian arrowwood''', or '''syringa,'''<ref name=ss>{{cite web|url=http://www.statesymbolsusa.org/Idaho/flower_syringa.html|title=State Symbols USA: Idaho State Flower|date=2 October 2014 }}</ref> is a [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] native to western North America, and is the [[List of U.S. state and territory flowers|state flower]] of [[Idaho]].

==Description==
The [[perennial]] shrub<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center - The University of Texas at Austin|url=https://www.wildflower.org/plants/result.php?id_plant=phle4|access-date=2022-01-01|website=www.wildflower.org}}</ref> is rounded and grows to {{convert|1.5-3|m|ft|abbr=off|sp=us|frac=2}} in height. It sends out long stems which are red when new and fade to gray with age, the bark shredding in small flakes.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|title=Mock Orange, Philadelphus lewisii|url=https://calscape.org/Philadelphus-lewisii-()|access-date=|website=calscape.org}}</ref>

The oppositely arranged leaves vary in size across individual plants but they are usually oval, {{convert|3|-|5|cm|frac=4|sp=us}} long, smooth or serrated along the edges, and light green in color with a rough texture.<ref name=":1" />

The flowers are produced in clusters at the ends of long stems, with four white petals up to {{convert|4|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long and numerous yellow [[stamen]]s. At the height of flowering, the plant is covered in a mass of blossoms. The flowers have a heavy, sweet scent similar to orange blossoms with a hint of pineapple.<ref name=":1" />

The [[fruit]] is a small hard [[capsule (fruit)|capsule]] about 1 cm long with woody, pointed wings, containing many brown seeds.<ref name="davesgarden" /> Drought will stunt fruit development and prevent the production of viable seeds.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Philadelphus lewisii|url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/philew/all.html#MANAGEMENT%20CONSIDERATIONS|access-date=2021-05-07|website=www.fs.fed.us}}</ref>

The plant is somewhat similar in appearance to [[serviceberry]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Taylor|first=Ronald J.|title=Sagebrush Country: A Wildflower Sanctuary|publisher=Mountain Press Pub. Co|year=1994|isbn=0-87842-280-3|edition=rev.|location=Missoula, MT|pages=166|language=en|oclc=25708726|orig-year=1992}}</ref>
[[File:Philadelphus lewisii (5192712320).jpg|thumb|Fruits]]

== Taxonomy ==
It was first collected for science by scientist and explorer [[Meriwether Lewis]] in 1806 during the [[Lewis and Clark Expedition]], and so was named after him.<ref name="USDA_boise_mockorange">{{cite web |title=Wildflowers - Syringa Philadelphus lewisii Hydrangea family |url=http://www.fs.usda.gov/r04/boise |access-date=23 March 2016 |publisher=USDA}}</ref><ref>Shaw, N. L. [http://www.fs.fed.us/global/iitf/pdf/shrubs/Philadelphus%20lewisii ''Philadelphus lewisii''.] In: Francis, J. K. (ed). ''Wildland Shrubs of the United States and its Territories: Thamnic Descriptions''. USDA Forest Service. GTR IITF-WB-1.</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
Lewis' mock-orange occurs from northwestern [[California]] in the [[Sierra Nevada (U.S.)|Sierra Nevada]], north through the [[Pacific Northwest]] to southern [[British Columbia]], and east to Idaho and [[Montana]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Philadelphus lewisii|url=https://www.wnps.org/native-plant-directory/184-philadelphus-lewisii|access-date=|website=www.wnps.org|language=en-us}}</ref> In the [[Cascade Range|Cascades]] it occurs from sea level up to {{Convert|7000|ft|m|abbr=on|order=flip}}, while in the [[Sierra Nevada]] it grows from {{Convert|1000-5000|ft|m|abbr=on|order=flip}}.<ref name=":0" />

Though it is tolerant of moderate shade, it prefers full sun. It is common in open coniferous forests and on forest edges, and in drier regions of the Northwest it occurs mostly in wetter and [[Riparian zone|riparian]] areas. It is also found in [[chaparral]] and [[Seral community|seral]] communities.<ref name=":0" />

It occurs on well-drained, moist sites, and is tolerant of rocky soil, and it is hardy from [[Hardiness zone|USDA zones]] 3 to 9.<ref name="davesgarden" /><ref name=":0" />

== Ecology ==
[[File:Philadelphus lewisii 1.jpg|thumb|in habitat in Washington state]]
The foliage of Lewis' mock orange is of moderate importance as winter forage for [[elk]] and [[deer]] in British Columbia, Idaho, and Montana. In Montana, a 1957 study found that it comprised 2% of [[mule deer]] diets in the winter and a trace in the summer.<ref name=":0" />

The seeds are eaten by [[quail]] and [[squirrel]]s.<ref name=":0" />

It occurs in dense shrub habitats which provide good thermal and security cover for wildlife.<ref name=":0" />

''Philadelphus lewisii'' is able to spread [[Vegetative reproduction|vegetatively]] and from seed. It forms [[Soil seed bank|seedbanks]] in the top {{Convert|2|in|cm|abbr=on|order=flip}} of soil.<ref name=":0" />

=== Fire ecology ===
The shrub is native to relatively arid regions of the American West which experience frequent [[Wildfires in the United States|wildfires]], and is therefore quite well adapted to fire. Although mock-orange is typically completely top-killed by fires, it will enthusiastically resprout from [[rhizome]]s and [[root crown]]s afterward.<ref name=":0" /> A 1971 study found that in the next growing season after a fire, mock-orange had already regrown to 50% of its previous diameter and height, and that those plants had an average of 28.9 to 38.0 sprouts per plant postfire compared to just 0.6 to 1.5 before.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Leege|first1=Thomas A.|last2=Hickey|first2=William O.|date=July 1971|title=Sprouting of Northern Idaho Shrubs after Prescribed Burning|url=http://dx.doi.org/10.2307/3799705|journal=The Journal of Wildlife Management|volume=35|issue=3|pages=508|doi=10.2307/3799705|jstor=3799705 |issn=0022-541X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Lewis' mock orange palatability for [[Rocky Mountain elk]] is much greater after fire, with 36.3% of twigs [[Browsing (herbivory)|browsed]] compared to only 1.3% on adjacent unburned sites.<ref name=":0" />

== Human use ==

===Ethnobotany===
Native American tribes use ''P. lewisii'' for numerous purposes. The hard wood is useful for making hunting and fishing tools, snowshoes, pipes, combs, cradles, [[Shuttle (weaving)|netting shuttles]], and furniture. The leaves and bark, which contain [[saponin]]s, are mixed in water for use as a mild soap.<ref name="bonner_2008" /><ref name="USDA_2003_mockorange">{{citation |url=https://plants.usda.gov/plantguide/pdf/pg_phle4.pdf|series=Plant guide|title=Lewis' Mockorange Philadelphus lewisii Pursh|date=21 November 2003|access-date=23 March 2016}}</ref> The flowers are used in preparing perfumes and teas.<ref name="bonner_2008">{{cite book|url=https://permanent.access.gpo.gov/LPS113557/LPS113557/www.nsl.fs.fed.us/nsl_wpsm.html|title=The Woody Plant Seed Manual|author=Bonner, Franklin T.|isbn=978-0-16-081131-9|date=July 2008|access-date=23 March 2016|location=Washington, DC|publisher=USDA|page=787}}</ref> The [[Syilx|Syilx/Okanagan]] people use ''P. lewisii'' blooming as a temporal sign that marmots are fat and ready to be hunted.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turner |first=Nancy J. |last2=Reid |first2=Andrea J. |date=November 7, 2026 |title=“When the Wild Roses Bloom”: Indigenous Knowledge and Environmental Change in Northwestern North America |url=https://agupubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1029/2022GH000612 |journal=GeoHealth |language=en |volume=6 |issue=11 |doi=10.1029/2022GH000612 |issn=2471-1403 |pmc=9665002 |pmid=36398276}}</ref> 

===Cultivation===
Lewis' mock-orange prefers full sun to partial sun. It is drought-tolerant, will grow in poor soils, and is suitable for [[xeriscaping]].<ref name=davesgarden>{{citation|url=http://davesgarden.com/guides/pf/go/94024/#b|work=Dave's Garden|access-date=23 March 2016|title=Waterton Mockorange Philadelphus lewisii Waterton}}</ref> It provides a landscape with flashy flowers and a fruity scent.[[File:Waterton Mockorange Philadelphus lewisii 'Waterton'.JPG|right|thumb|Waterton Mockorange ''Philadelphus lewisii 'Waterton''']]

The Waterton Mockorange ''Philadelphus lewisii 'Waterton''' was hybridized by the Alberta Horticultural Research Station in [[Brooks, Alberta]], Canada. It grows to {{Convert|1.2-1.8|m|ft|abbr=on|frac=2}} in height. It is named for [[Augustus Griffin]], who in 1933 noted that this plant was growing in what is now [[Waterton Lakes National Park]] in Canada.<ref name="davesgarden" />

== In culture ==
''Philadelphus lewisii'' is the state flower of Idaho.<ref name="ss" /> The plant is protected by Idaho state law along with other native wildflowers and shrubs, and it is illegal to collect wild specimens on public property for export, sale, or transport without approval.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Section 18-3911 – Idaho State Legislature|url=https://legislature.idaho.gov/statutesrules/idstat/title18/t18ch39/sect18-3911/|access-date=2021-05-07|language=en-US}}</ref>
